The variance between runs is GC timing, not the graph or the 'deleted' files.

Across four runs on the same code, window restores were 0, 4 322, 13 684 and 13 803. The decode predicts about 13.7k for a fully cold file EAVT plus branches plus AVET :file/path. Each run has only one restore-conn phase, so the conn was not re-restored. The :deleted-3 runs split 4.3k versus 13.7k, so the deletes do not explain it.

investigation.experiment:
E1, which cuts the reconcile question, needs no code change. Run a reopen of prof-10k-s3 with the harness attached to the renderer's DedicatedWorker target over CDP. Call HeapProfiler.collectGarbage on it right after the LSPERF initial-data record appears. Then sum the restores and max-lag in the activity windows until the pulls stop. Do 3 runs with and 3 without the forced GC.
- Prediction if WeakRef eviction is the cause: with GC, about 13-14k restores and multi-second max-lag every time; without GC, 0 to 13.8k, varying.
- If the forced-GC runs stay near 0, WeakRef is refuted, and the cold pulls need another cause before any "fetch content lazily later" plan is trusted.

E2, which cuts the initial-data question, needs one flag. Add a flag that switches only the file part of get-initial-data (initial_data.cljs:362) to AVET :file/path datoms plus the full EAVT of the 3 boot files. Log three timings for each part: sync-ms, total-ms−sync-ms and the UI restore.cljs:36 time. Run it on/off, 3 times each, on prof-10k-s3.
- Prediction from the decode: datoms 93.0k → about 72.9k, restores 18.4k → about 17.8k, sync −0.3 to −0.9 s, the post-sync gap −0.7 to −1.0 s.

investigation.proposal:
Principle: nothing below touches page identity. The UI page set stays byte-identical.

0. MEASURE (no behaviour change)
- Time get-initial-data in its parts: idents / files / pages / distinct.
- Log the transit-write ms separately from sync-ms.
- Dump `*profile` per activity window (thread_api.cljc:24,73), so the 10k reconcile pulls become visible.

1. FILES OUT OF THE BOOT REPLY (the safe part of phase 1)
- For file graphs, `all-files` becomes the AVET :file/path datoms plus the full EAVT of logseq/config.edn, custom.css and custom.js.
- Skip recent-updated-pages for file graphs. Its 15 pages are already in the page set, and updated-at is stripped (383-386).
- Gain from the decode: −20 116 datoms, −6.9 MB of content in the reply, about −600 restores. Estimated −1.0 to −2.0 s of the ~10 s continuous worker block, plus a smaller UI conn build.
- This is NOT substantial on its own; say so when it lands.
- Consumers to handle in the same change:
  1. Save path (file_based/file.cljs:110, :270; fs/node.cljs:40): fetch the old content from the worker with `<get-file`, awaited BEFORE set-file-content! is sent (alter-files 272-279). Or have the worker attach it to :write-files.
  2. components/file.cljs:108: in-db? from `db/file-exists?`; the path datoms stay.
  3. code.cljs:60: `<get-file`.
  4. native_fs.cljs:243/171-188 (Refresh/re-index): pull path, mtime and content through a worker `<q {:transact-db? false}`.
  5. developer.cljs:87-90 and page_menu.cljs:171-173: `<get-file`.
  6. file_based/events.cljs:330-332 and fs/sync.cljs:1551: gate them if Logseq Sync is unreachable in this fork, else convert them to `<get-file`.
  7. Decide the three leak paths explicitly. Simplest safe choice: leave them (reconcile will refill the UI db), but write the tests with them plugged, so missed consumers show up.

2. BOUND THE STALL, NOT THE WORK (the only no-identity lever that cuts the stall substantially)
- Make thread-api/get-initial-data async:
  - capture `db = @conn` once;
  - walk AVET :block/name in chunks under a time budget (25-50 ms), yielding between chunks (setTimeout/MessageChannel);
  - build the same seq and return it at the end.
- Output is identical, so none of the 229 UI page-lookup sites and no identity path changes.
- Max worker stall drops from about 8.5 s to the budget plus one transit write (smaller after step 1).
- Honest limit: the UI waits for the whole set, so time until the UI db exists stays around 10 s at 10k. The work stays linear.
- Guards:
  - assert that `(:max-tx @conn)` is unchanged at the end (the UI has no conn yet to receive txs);
  - one walk per repo;
  - accept that WeakRef eviction adds a few branch re-restores per chunk.

3. RECONCILE
- Now: cap the p/all at watcher_handler.cljs:186-197 at about 16-32 in flight. Same semantics, and no 10k-deep queue.
- Then: a `<get-file` that returns content without transacting it into the UI conn.
- Bounded version (ADR-003 step): persist :file/last-modified-at and :file/size on every parse and write (today 3 of 10 060 files have an mtime, none a size). Reconcile then becomes stat-only plus one batched worker call over (path, mtime, size), in chunks with a cursor. Only changed files are read and compared. The first run after the change backfills.
- Whatever you land: count the reconcile's restores separately. Because of WeakRef they are not "already paid by initial-data".

4. PREREQUISITES FOR BOUNDING THE PAGE SET (the only change that bounds the work; not to implement now)
- a) Worker-side page-ref resolution at the UI write entry points: apply-ops! :save-block, :insert-blocks and :transact, and thread-api/transact.
  - Keep :block/name on rewritten refs. Otherwise remove-orphaned-page-refs! (/home/johan/dev/logsidian-perf/deps/outliner/src/logseq/outliner/core.cljs:69) plus get-orphaned-pages (/home/johan/dev/logsidian-perf/deps/db/src/logseq/db.cljs:375) retract ref-only pages. There are 488 of them at 10k.
  - Rewrite top-level maps only when they carry a uuid that is absent from the db (whiteboard saves have none).
  - Preserve title and created-at, which block.cljs:323 and 351-354 would otherwise overwrite.
- b) Move remove-non-existed-refs! (/home/johan/dev/logsidian-perf/src/main/frontend/handler/file_based/editor.cljs:34, applied at 133) into the worker.
- c) Resolve query-DSL page refs by name in the worker (/home/johan/dev/logsidian-perf/src/main/frontend/db/query_dsl.cljs:499,508), including uuid-string refs (db.cljs:326).
- d) Nil-guard home-page? in <delete! (/home/johan/dev/logsidian-perf/src/main/frontend/handler/common/page.cljs:167-172).
- e) Watcher file→page lookups in the worker (watcher_handler.cljs:105,181,189).
- f) An enumerated audit plus a lint allowlist of UI sync page lookups (229 hits per the step-3 critique, plus db-utils/pull, pull-many and react/q). Include the `<q` cache with :transact-db? true.
- g) Identity tests:
  - a block that is the sole referrer of a ref-only page, saved with the ref kept → the page survives;
  - a whiteboard save through :transact;
  - typing [[Existing]] with an empty UI db keeps uuid, title and created-at.
- Useful fact: 10 000 of 10 542 pages at 10k are journals, and their uuids are derived from journal-day (block.cljs:337-338). Resolving them in the worker is exact; the hard cases are the 540 other pages, 488 of them ref-only.
investigation.risks:
- Step 1:
  - Any missed reader of `db/get-file` silently gets nil. The worst case is spurious logseq/bak files on save (fs/node.cljs:40 → 45-46) and lost raw-file edits (components/file.cljs:108 → code.cljs:72 global path).
  - The three leak paths refill content, so manual testing after boot can pass while the first ~20 s after reopen, or a file never pulled, fails. Test with the leaks plugged.
  - Refresh/re-index misdetects every file as changed until native_fs is converted.
- Step 2:
  - Any worker transact between the snapshot and the UI conn is lost to the UI. Today's code has the same exposure for about 1.5 s; slicing widens it to about 10 s. Verify nothing writes the conn then (electron watcher events before `:graph/ready`?).
  - A promise-returning get-initial-data changes thread-api timing, and a graph switch in the middle of a walk must be handled.
  - Slicing improves the stall metric, not time-to-UI. Do not report it as a latency win.
- Step 3:
  - A concurrency cap lengthens the reconcile's wall time (it already runs in the background).
  - mtime-based reconcile misses edits that keep mtime and size (rare; the first run after the change still does a full compare).
- WeakRef eviction means any "moved to after boot" estimate is nondeterministic. Every A/B needs several runs, and reconcile restores must be reported separately.
- The step-3 design's gain (4.5-7.5 s) and its "~41 MB content" are contradicted by the decode. The critique's "phase 1 moves the content restores to load-graph-files!" holds only for the 594 file-only leaves; the larger re-restore comes from GC.

critique.wrong_claims:
1. H1's premise, "four runs on the same code", is false. Checked in bench/run-{after,step3,now}.sh and in the logs:
- The runs span three builds: after/reopen-10k is step 2 (linked refs still 6 042 ms), the two step3 runs are step 3, and now/reopen-10k is step 3 plus the NOW fast path (q-fastpath lines).
- They span two profiles: prof-10k for now, after and step3/reopen-10k; prof-10k-s3 for the 0-restore run (run-step3.sh:57).
- The only 0-restore run is therefore also the only different profile and the only `:deleted 0` run. It is confounded on profile, build and deletes at once.
- The decode (prof-10k-s3) is compared with restore counts from prof-10k. prof-10k ships 93 026 datoms against 93 013.
- The s3 decode is of the post-run file with the WAL applied, so it includes that session's writes. Its "3 absolute :file/path datoms" do not contradict `:deleted 0`: the s3 reopen itself transacts the global config file (apply-outliner-ops :transact at harness ts 34120).

2. H5 has two errors:
- journals/1999_07_20.md is 16 bytes on disk, not "about 0.7 KB".
- "Not the first journal, so not the first cold access" contradicts H1. If the tree is warm after boot and a GC evicts it later, the first cold access is whichever pull follows that GC. 1999_07_20.md is #86 in reconcile order, and the first restores of the reconcile (1204 in the window ending t=33776) are exactly there. The simplest reading is that the 326 ms pull is the evicting major GC pause plus root and branch re-restores. H5 is the same event as H1, not a separate hypothesis.

3. H2's own evidence argues against a "10k-deep queue":
- In the warm s3 reconcile the same uncapped p/all ran for about 30 s with max-lag of only 51–205 ms.
- If 10k pulls sat queued ahead of the heartbeat, the warm run would stall too.
- So the queue depth is limited by how fast pulls arrive (two IPC calls, a UI db/file-exists? and a UI transact per file). Cold adds only about 1.4 restores, or about 0.6 ms, per pull on average. The multi-second lag then needs service time to cross the arrival rate, which has not been shown.
- Also, heartbeat lag is not an artifact. Any UI request queued behind the pulls waits just as long.

4. E2 and proposal step 1 likely overstate the gain after the sync timer:
- The transit write in thread_api.cljc:92 has a per-datom handler cost. The 6.9 MB of strings is cheap in JSON.stringify.
- Dropping 21.6 % of the datoms suggests about −0.3 s of the 1.29–1.41 s gap, not −0.7 to −1.0 s. The claim "content is most of the reply bytes, so most of the cost" is assumed, not measured.

5. E2's metric "UI restore.cljs:36 time" does not exist. That log/info line appears 0 times in the release console logs (glogi is off), so it needs a console.log.

6. The 711–890 ms UI task (now 835, after 890, step3 848, s3 711) is attributed only to conn-from-datoms.
- get-initial-data is called without direct-pass (persist_db/browser.cljs:224-231), so the UI thread also transit-reads the full reply, content included.

7. "E1 cuts the reconcile question" is wrong:
- E1 does not test H2 at all.

hypotheses.claim: WAL auto-checkpoint inside the committing transaction. It copies about 1000 frames (8 MB) into the main file and calls sah.flush (fsync) 2-3 times: WAL before, db after, WAL header at restart. This sets the floor of the slow slices (roughly 100-200 ms).
hypotheses.evidence_for: Counts match. About 170 checkpoints per walk (ckpt_seq 341 over two walks) vs 186 slow slices over 125 ms. On first open, 213 checkpoints vs 159 files over 150 ms and 285 over 100 ms. Cadence fits: 26.8 frames per commit gives one checkpoint every ~37 commits. Commit-ms does not track rows (r=0.08) and does not grow with index size. Under NORMAL + exclusive WAL, sah.flush runs only at checkpoints and restarts, so every fsync lands in the committing slice. Commit-ms clusters at 100-150 ms (104 of 258 slices).
hypotheses.evidence_against: There is no per-commit proof yet: no wal_hook binding exists, and checkpoint cost on this disk is unmeasured. At one checkpoint per ~37 commits, it cannot explain all 258 slow slices (median gap 18). The ckpt_seq attribution assumes the WAL survived every session, which the 79.5 MB file surviving since the 01:45 rebuild supports.

hypotheses.claim: FTS5 automerge/crisismerge running inline, amplified because every upsert statement flushes its own level-0 segment (one segment per row). This produces the upper tail (250-725 ms).
hypotheses.evidence_for: The replay reproduces the app's writeCounter exactly (72,928). Native in memory, without I/O, it gives tx p99 46 ms and max 97-133 ms, with 130-140 events per walk; a wasm factor of 1.5-3x puts that at 70-400 ms. The spikes sit in the upsert phase, which the app reports as commit-ms. With automerge=0 plus idle merges the tail disappears (max 16.5 ms). Merge output also adds WAL frames, which brings checkpoints sooner.
hypotheses.evidence_against: The wasm/native factor is assumed. The replay has no WAL, so the I/O part of a merge is missing. Batching rows into one statement alone leaves the tail (p99 56 ms), so segment count is not the whole story.

hypotheses.claim: Linux writeback and fsync latency variance amplify the checkpoint cost. A walk writes about 1.2 GB of WAL plus about 1.2 GB of checkpoint copies with no fsync at commit, so dirty-page throttling and slow fsyncs come in bursts.
hypotheses.evidence_for: The slow slices over 200 ms come in clusters (11 in about 6 s, including 609 and 725), which fits I/O contention better than deterministic merges.
hypotheses.evidence_against: Nothing was measured at the OS level, and merge cascades can also cluster.

hypotheses.claim: Trigger cost. On the walk: indirect only. On the edit path at HEAD: the delete-by-id trigger scans the whole FTS table.
hypotheses.evidence_for: Edit path: the query plan shows `SCAN blocks_fts VIRTUAL TABLE INDEX 0:`. That costs 31-69 ms native per changed row and 614 ms for 20 deleted blocks, O(N), on every edit, and it is already fixed in the working tree. On the walk the rows are all inserts after the truncate, so the insert trigger adds little by itself. The real cost is that each row is its own statement, hence its own segment.

investigation.experiment:
One bench-only run of the existing now/reindex-10k scenario: LSBENCH_REINDEX=1 on prof-10k, about 4 minutes. It measures the ranking directly, with no A/B needed.

1. In commit-batch! and sync-rows!, replace `.transaction` with explicit steps: BEGIN, the row statements (timed as upsert-ms), the meta write, then COMMIT (timed as commit-ms).

2. Make checkpoints observable. Set `PRAGMA wal_autocheckpoint=0` on the search db, then run `PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(PASSIVE)` every 37 commits. That reproduces today's ~1000-frame cadence, measured at 26.8 frames/commit. Time it (ckpt-ms) and log its result row [busy, log, checkpointed]: log is the WAL frame count.

3. Detect FTS5 merges cheaply. Before and after each transaction, run `SELECT block FROM blocks_fts_data WHERE id=10` (a rowid lookup). Decode nSegment and writeCounter: varints after a 4-byte cookie, or 8 bytes if bytes 4-7 are ff000001. A drop in nSegment, or a level change, means a merge ran.

4. Log per slice over 50 ms: rows, upsert-ms, commit-ms, ckpt-ms, wal-frames, nseg-before and nseg-after, and leaves flushed. Log the same fields per sync-tx! in the typing run (LSBENCH_TYPE=40).

Decision rule:
- ckpt-ms p50 at or above 100 ms, and slow slices without a checkpoint dropping by more than half: hypothesis 1 is confirmed.
- Remaining spikes in upsert-ms coinciding with nSegment drops: hypothesis 2.
- Neither: I/O jitter, or something else.

Optional second run, to confirm the fix: add `INSERT INTO blocks_fts(blocks_fts, rank) VALUES('automerge',0)` and `('crisismerge',64)`, and expect the upper tail to go.
investigation.proposal:
Smallest safe changes first. Keep what is already in the working tree: rowid triggers, no-op upsert skip, schema-v2 migration.

1. One statement per commit (no migration needed).
   - Validate rows in JS as upsert-row! does today, then write them with one statement: `INSERT INTO blocks(id,title,page) SELECT value->>0, value->>1, value->>2 FROM json_each($rows) WHERE true ON CONFLICT(id) DO UPDATE SET title=excluded.title, page=excluded.page WHERE blocks.title IS NOT excluded.title OR blocks.page IS NOT excluded.page`.
   - Write the meta row first. Use one `DELETE ... IN` for removals.
   - Result: one FTS5 segment per commit instead of one per row. In the replay, 3.2x fewer leaves and 31% less total time.
   - Crash safety is unchanged: it is still one transaction.

2. Take FTS5 merges off the commit path.
   - Set `INSERT INTO blocks_fts(blocks_fts, rank) VALUES('automerge', 0)` and `VALUES('crisismerge', 64)`. These persist in blocks_fts_config. Set them in create-tables-and-triggers! for new tables and once on open for existing ones.
   - Add an idle merge step to the indexer's idle gate (≥1 s without a thread-api call, reusing busy?): `INSERT INTO blocks_fts(blocks_fts, rank) VALUES('merge', 64)`, repeated while `total_changes()` still moves, each call about 25 ms.
   - Result: native replay p99 goes from 46 to 8.5 ms and max from 97 to 16.5 ms. The same merge work (3.6 s native per 70k rows) moves to idle time.
   - Crash safety: each merge is its own transaction. If idle never comes, crisismerge=64 bounds the level-0 segment count; searches pay a few extra ms per query for those segments.

3. Take WAL checkpoints off the commit path, next to db_worker.cljs:358.
   - Set `PRAGMA wal_autocheckpoint=0` and `PRAGMA journal_size_limit=16777216` on the search db only.
   - Run `PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(PASSIVE)` from the same idle scheduler once about 500 or more frames have accumulated. Use the returned log count, or count commits at about 27 frames each.
   - Add a hard cap: at 8000 or more frames (64 MB), checkpoint right after the commit anyway.
   - Crash safety is the same as today. In WAL + NORMAL, committed transactions survive a process kill whether or not they have been checkpointed. A power loss can drop the last unsynced commits, which is already accepted and healed through the watermark gap (truncate and walk).
   - Cost: the total I/O is unchanged but runs in idle time. A checkpoint still blocks the worker for about 100-200 ms, but only after 1 s of quiet. Recovery at open reads at most 64 MB of WAL. journal_size_limit shrinks today's 79 MB WAL file.

4. Fold into the pending v2 migration, so that only one rebuild ever happens: `fts5(id UNINDEXED, title, page UNINDEXED, tokenize="trigram")`. No query matches on id or page, and the `page = ?` filter still works on an UNINDEXED column. Result: 38% smaller index, fewer WAL frames per commit, fewer checkpoints and less merge work.

5. Afterwards, include the commit in the slice budget. With the spikes gone, next-batch-size (search_indexer HEAD:52) grows batches from about 12 rows toward 1024, which means fewer commits per row.

Only if measurement still shows fsync-bound checkpoints: `synchronous=OFF` on the search db. That removes the fsyncs, but a power loss could then corrupt the file. It first needs a corruption heal path: on SQLITE_CORRUPT, delete the search db through the pool and rebuild. create-tables-and-triggers! currently swallows errors with a FIXME (working tree search.cljs:163-171).
investigation.risks:
- **Replay vs. the app:** the replay is native 3.46.1, in memory, while the app runs wasm 3.50.3 on OPFS. Absolute ms will differ. The mechanisms (per-statement segment flush, the id scan) were confirmed, and writeCounter matches exactly.
- **Checkpoint cost is unmeasured:** it could be much smaller or larger than 100-200 ms on another disk or on Windows.
- **automerge=0 without idle time:** segments build up to the crisismerge bound, and each search pays a little extra. A 64-segment crisis merge is small but still happens inline.
- **Deferred checkpoints:** the WAL grows up to the cap, so reopen recovery and memory use for the heap wal-index in exclusive mode grow with it. The cap must stay.

   - On first open (about 1723 s of continuous thread-api calls, so the ≥1 s idle gate may never open), level 1 reaches 64 segments after about 4096 commits, then is merged inline in one go. That is a multi-second stall, the opposite of ADR-003.
   - The claim "a 64-segment crisis merge is small" holds only at level 0.
   - The merge work needs a bounded step that runs in every slice (e.g. `'merge', -N` with small N), not only in idle time.

4. The proposal's 8000-frame checkpoint cap would, in busy periods such as first open, turn every checkpoint into a 64 MB inline copy, about 8x today's. The cap should stay near 1000 frames, or checkpoints should run at slice boundaries whether or not the worker is idle.

5. Checkpoint I/O can be measured without a wal_hook. In the worker, wrap FileSystemSyncAccessHandle.prototype.flush, write and truncate. Under WAL + NORMAL, any flush during a commit means a checkpoint or a WAL restart.

6. The main db checkpoints too (prof-10k ckpt_seq 354, prof-10k-s3 352). That belongs on the first-open and store-ms side, not in search-ms.

7. Running the experiment on the working tree triggers the schema-v2 "schema" rebuild and changes the triggers (explicit rowids). The build must be pinned: HEAD, or the working tree deliberately.
critique.better_experiment:
The proposed experiment does not cleanly separate the hypotheses. Four problems:
- Step 2 changes the system under test. It disables autocheckpoint and checkpoints every 37 commits, a cadence taken from non-walk WAL data. Merges write bursts of frames, so today checkpoints tend to land in merge-heavy commits; a fixed commit-count cadence breaks that link and cannot show it.
- The decision rule ("slow slices without a checkpoint drop by more than half") has no baseline, because the current log is cut off at 100 ms.
- A drop in nSegment misses incremental automerge work: nSeg changes only when a merge finishes, and writeCounter counts flushed leaves, not merge output. So "no nSegment drop" does not mean "no merge".
- H3 is left as whatever remains unexplained.

Better, with no change to SQLite settings (autocheckpoint stays at its default), on a pinned HEAD bench build:
1. In the worker, wrap FileSystemSyncAccessHandle.prototype.write, flush and truncate to count calls, bytes and ms into a global counter.
2. In commit-batch! and sync-rows!, split the transaction into timed steps: BEGIN, upserts (upsert-ms), meta write, COMMIT (commit-ms).
3. Log EVERY slice, not just those over 100 ms. Fields:
   - rows and total title chars;
   - upsert-ms and commit-ms;
   - write-ms and write-bytes;
   - flush-count and flush-ms (flush > 0 means a checkpoint or WAL restart under NORMAL);
   - truncate-ms;
   - total_changes() delta minus rows (FTS shadow-table writes, i.e. merge work including partial automerge steps);
   - a per-level segment summary from the blocks_fts_data id=10 record.
4. Classify each slow slice from those fields:
   - H1 (checkpoint I/O): a flush in the slice, and I/O time covers most of the slice.
   - H2 (merge CPU): a large shadow-write delta, with CPU time (slice minus I/O) dominant.
   - H3 (writeback): I/O time is high without checkpoint-sized writes. Sample /proc/meminfo Dirty/Writeback in memwatch.py at the same time.
5. Run the walk twice to check that the late cluster at eid 90k+ reproduces.
6. Then run once with bounded per-slice `'merge'` plus a small checkpoint cap to confirm the fix. Also run a first-open segment, which never goes idle, to check that no crisis-merge or cap stall appears.
